problems.title: Printing text and calculated results
problems.prompt: This calculation assumes you upload 4 videos a day for 30 days and each video gets 2,500 views. Predict the four lines of output without running the code.
hints: Text inside quotes prints exactly as written. An expression without quotes prints its calculated value.
Estimate the last line first. Is 120 times 2500 in the tens of thousands or the hundreds of thousands?
problems.explain:
Text in quotes prints exactly as written, and an expression without quotes prints its value. `4 * 30` is 120, and multiplying that by 2500 gives 300000.
It is easy to write the last line with commas, like 300,000, or to drop a zero. Python prints large numbers without commas. If you estimate about 300,000 before you run the code, you will notice a wrong number of digits right away.
problems.code:
print("Videos uploaded in a month")
print(4 * 30)
print("Views received in a month")
print(4 * 30 * 2500)

expect.stdout:
Videos uploaded in a month
120
Views received in a month
300000
expect.screen:
Videos uploaded in a month
120
Views received in a month
300000

problems.solution:
print("Videos uploaded in a month")
print(4 * 30)
print("Views received in a month")
print(4 * 30 * 2500)

problems.title: A cell that prints a name
problems.prompt: You wrote the code below in one cell. Without running it, predict what the cell prints when it runs.
hints: Compare the name on the fourth line with the name given on the second line, letter by letter.
Python runs the code one line at a time from the top and stops at the line where an error occurs.
problems.explain:
The second line gives the name `views` to 2400, but the fourth line tries to print `view`, which is missing the s. That name was never given a value, so the code stops with `NameError: name 'view' is not defined`. The two lines of output before it have already been printed, and the last line, `print("Done")`, does not run.
It is easy to think that nothing prints when there is an error and leave the answer empty, or to think that Python will use the similar name `views` for you. Look at the name that the last line of the error message points to, and you will see right away what to fix.
problems.code:
print("Today's log")
views = 2400
print(views)
print(view)
print("Done")
problems.solution:
print("Today's log")
views = 2400
print(views)
print(view)
print("Done")

problems.title: The run order decides the value
problems.prompt: A notebook has four cells. From the top, we call them cell 1, cell 2, cell 3, and cell 4. You ran them in this order: cell 4, cell 3, cell 1, cell 2, cell 3. The code below joins the cells in the order they ran. Lines that start with `#` are notes that say which cell each part is, so they do not run. Predict the output of each run, in order.
hints: Cell 4 is at the bottom of the notebook, but you ran it first.
Anything in quotes is text, not a name.
problems.explain:
A notebook remembers what happened in the order the cells ran, not by where the cells sit in the document. Cell 4 ran first, so the first `likes` printed is 95, and after cell 1 runs, the value printed again is 70. Cell 2 prints the text likes inside the quotes as it is.
Because cell 1 is at the top of the document, it is easy to assume that `likes` is 70 from the start, or to read the likes inside the quotes as a value too and write 95, 70, 70. When the output is not what you expected, check the order the cells ran before you look at where they sit.
problems.code:
# Cell 4
likes = 95
# Cell 3
print(likes)
# Cell 1
likes = 70
# Cell 2
print("likes")
# Cell 3 (run again)
print(likes)
problems.solution:
# Cell 4
likes = 95
# Cell 3
print(likes)
# Cell 1
likes = 70
# Cell 2
print("likes")
# Cell 3 (run again)
print(likes)

problems.title: A notebook that stops on Run all
problems.prompt: Yesterday this notebook worked because you ran the cells one at a time, in an order you chose. Today you opened it again and used "Run all" to run the cells in order from the top, and it stopped with an error in cell 2. The code below joins the cells of the notebook from the top. Lines that start with `#` are notes that say which cell each part is. Move just one cell so that running from the top prints `Subscribers` and then `350`. Grading runs the code again with a different number of subscribers.
hints: Which name does the last line of the error message say Python does not know?
Where in the document is the cell that gives that name its value?
problems.explain:
"Run all" runs the cells in order from the top of the document. When cell 2 tries to print `subscribers`, cell 3, which gives that name its value, has not run yet, so you get a NameError. Move cell 3 above cell 2, or move cell 2 to the bottom. Yesterday there was no error only because you had run cell 3 first.
If you write the value directly, as in `print(350)`, it looks right for now, but the wrong value stays when the number of subscribers changes. Arrange the cells so that running them all from the top gives the same result. Then you can reuse the notebook as it is, even after the session ends.
problems.code:
# Cell 1
print("Subscribers")
# Cell 2
print(subscribers)
# Cell 3
subscribers = 350
problems.solution:
# Cell 3
subscribers = 350
# Cell 1
print("Subscribers")
# Cell 2
print(subscribers)

problems.title: An answer that says to reinstall
problems.prompt: A notebook you made yesterday has three cells. Cell 1 has `likes = 310`, cell 2 has `comments = 42`, and cell 3 prints the two values in order. Today you opened the notebook again and ran only cells 1 and 3, and cell 3 stopped with an error. When you told an AI only "Python suddenly stopped working," it suggested reinstalling Python. The code below joins the cells you ran today, in the order you ran them. Without reinstalling anything, add the line `comments = 42` from cell 2 in the right place (just that one line) so that the code prints `310` and `42`. Grading runs the code again with both values changed.
hints: Which name does the last line of the error message say Python does not know?
Even if a cell is in the document, the session does not remember it unless you ran it today.
problems.explain:
The last line, `NameError: name 'comments' is not defined`, means the current session has no name `comments`. It has nothing to do with installation. Cell 2 is still in the document, but you did not run it today. Add cell 2's line `comments = 42` before cell 3.
When an AI does not know your situation, it gives general advice that only sounds right. Before you ask, read the last line of the error first. When you ask, include that line and describe your situation, as in "Today I ran only cells 1 and 3." If you change `print(comments)` to `print(42)`, it looks right for now, but it becomes wrong when the number of comments changes.
problems.code:
# Cell 1
likes = 310
# Cell 3
print(likes)
print(comments)
problems.solution:
# Cell 1
likes = 310
# Cell 2
comments = 42
# Cell 3
print(likes)
print(comments)

problems.title: Changing the number of likes
problems.prompt: You changed `likes` from 120 to 200. Predict the output without running the code.
hints: Look separately at the calculation that uses the variable and the text inside the quotes.
problems.explain: `likes + 5` uses the 200 stored in the variable, so it gives 205. `"Likes"` prints the text written in the code as it is, so it stays the same when you change `likes`.
problems.code:
likes = 200
print(likes + 5)
print("Likes")
problems.solution:
likes = 200
print(likes + 5)
print("Likes")

problems.title: Calculating again from the current value
problems.prompt: Predict the three lines of output without running the code.
hints: An assignment calculates the right side first.
What data type does `/` return, even when the numbers divide evenly?
problems.explain:
`score = score + 5` first calculates `80 + 5` on the right side and then stores the result back in `score`. Adding two integers gives an `int`, and `6 / 2` gives 3.0 (a `float`) even though it divides evenly.
In Colab, if you run only the second line onward again, `score` starts from its current value, 85, and becomes 90. To go back to the starting value, run the code again from `score = 80`.
problems.code:
score = 80
score = score + 5
print(score)
print(type(score))
print(6 / 2)
problems.solution:
score = 80
score = score + 5
print(score)
print(type(score))
print(6 / 2)

problems.title: + and * change with the data type
problems.prompt: Predict the three lines of output without running the code.
hints: Anything in quotes is a string, even if it looks like a number.
problems.explain:
Between two numbers, `+` adds, so you get 5. Between two strings, `+` joins them, so you get 23, and `"2" * 3` repeats the string three times to give 222.
What an operator does depends on the data types of the values on both sides of it.
problems.code:
print(2 + 3)
print("2" + "3")
print("2" * 3)
problems.solution:
print(2 + 3)
print("2" + "3")
print("2" * 3)

problems.title: Telling numbers from text
problems.prompt: Predict the three lines of output without running the code.
hints: A space counts as one character too.
problems.explain: `"12" * 3` repeats the string `"12"` three times, and `12 * 3` multiplies two integers. `"Social AI"` has 8 letters and 1 space, so its length is 9. Without the space, it would be 8.
problems.code:
print("12" * 3)
print(12 * 3)
print(len("Social AI"))
problems.solution:
print("12" * 3)
print(12 * 3)
print(len("Social AI"))

problems.title: Taking the city and the year out of a string
problems.prompt: Print the first character of `s`, its last character, the city name before the underscore, the year after the underscore, and the whole string reversed, one per line in that order. Use indexing and slicing.
hints: Draw tick marks between the characters, starting at 0. The last character is -1.
The character at the end position of a slice is not included. To go all the way to the end, leave the end empty.
problems.explain: `s[0]` is the first character and `s[-1]` is the last. `s[:5]` covers positions 0 through 4, so it is Seoul, and `s[6:]` runs from position 6 to the end, so it is 2026. `s[::-1]` reads one character at a time from the back, which reverses the string.
problems.code: s = "Seoul_2026"
problems.solution:
s = "Seoul_2026"
print(s[0])
print(s[-1])
print(s[:5])
print(s[6:])
print(s[::-1])

problems.title: A sentence from an age and a year
problems.prompt: Using the variables that hold an age and the current year, print the sentence `I am 20 years old, and the current year is 2026.` Use an f-string.
hints: If you put `f` before the quotes, you can put variable names inside braces.
problems.explain: An f-string has `f` before the quotes, and you write a variable name, such as `{age}`, where its value should go. You do not need to convert the numbers with `str()`.

require.message: Use an f-string by putting `f` before the quotes.

problems.code:
age = 20
year = 2026
problems.solution:
age = 20
year = 2026
print(f"I am {age} years old, and the current year is {year}.")

expect.stdout: I am 20 years old, and the current year is 2026.
I am 19 years old, and the current year is 2027.

problems.title: Reviewing variables, slices, and data types
problems.prompt: Predict the three lines of output without running the code.
hints: Is the 120 inside the quotes a number?
problems.explain: `likes + 5` uses the stored number, so it gives 125. `text[:5]` covers positions 0 through 4, so it is Seoul. `"120"` is in quotes, so it is a string, and its data type is `str`.
problems.code:
likes = 120
print(likes + 5)
text = "Seoul_2026"
print(text[:5])
print(type("120"))
problems.solution:
likes = 120
print(likes + 5)
text = "Seoul_2026"
print(text[:5])
print(type("120"))

problems.title: Reactions and the reaction rate
problems.prompt: The number of likes is stored in the string `likes_text`. Store the number of reactions, which is the number of likes plus the number of comments, in `reactions`. Divide the number of reactions by the number of views, multiply by 100, and store the result in `rate`. Print `reactions` and `rate` on two lines. Show `rate` to one decimal place and put `%` after it.
hints: Convert the string `"120"` with `int()` before you add it.
`f"{rate:.1f}%"` shows one decimal place and adds `%` at the end.
problems.explain:
`likes_text` is a string, so you must convert it with `int()` before you can add it. There are 128 reactions, no matter how many views there are.
When the views double from 1600 to 3200, the rate halves from 8.0% to 4.0%. This rate is the number of reactions divided by the number of views. It is not the share of people who reacted.
problems.code:
likes_text = "120"
comments = 8
views = 3200
problems.solution:
likes_text = "120"
comments = 8
views = 3200
likes = int(likes_text)
reactions = likes + comments
rate = reactions / views * 100
print(reactions)
print(f"{rate:.1f}%")

problems.title: Fixing code that prints a name and an age
problems.prompt: This code tries to print a name, its first letter, and an age. It has four mistakes, so it stops with an error. Fix it so that it prints `Kim(K): age 19`. The age is the difference in years and ignores birthdays.
hints: If you write only `int(birth)`, where does the converted value go?
Look at the index of the first letter, the `f` before the quotes, and the place where a string and a number are added.
problems.explain:
You need to store the result of `int(birth)` back in `birth` to get an integer. The first letter is `name[0]`; `name[1]` is the second letter.
To put values inside braces, add `f` before the quotes. Adding an integer to a string with `+` raises a TypeError, so put the calculation inside the f-string too.
problems.code:
name = "Kim"
birth = "2007"
int(birth)
first = name[1]
print("{name}({first}): age "
      + (2026 - birth))
problems.solution:
name = "Kim"
birth = "2007"
birth = int(birth)
first = name[0]
print(f"{name}({first}): age {2026 - birth}")

problems.title: A slice that is off by one
problems.prompt: This code tries to take out the year 2026. Predict the two lines of output without running the code.
hints: At which index is the last 6 of 2026?
problems.explain:
The character at the end position of a slice is not included. `s[6:9]` covers the characters at positions 6, 7, and 8, so it is 202, and the 6 at position 9 is left out. To take out the whole year, use `s[6:10]` or `s[6:]` with the end left empty.
This off-by-one error comes from mixing up the index of the last character (9) with the tick mark after the last character (10).
problems.code:
s = "Seoul_2026"
print(s[6:9])
print(s[6:10])
problems.solution:
s = "Seoul_2026"
print(s[6:9])
print(s[6:10])

problems.title: Printing a list and counting it
problems.prompt: This is the list of tags on a post. Predict the three lines of output without running the code.
hints: When you print a whole list, the square brackets and commas are printed too. What kind of quotes do the strings inside it show up with?
`len()` counts the items in a list and the characters in a string.
problems.explain:
`print(tags)` prints the whole list, square brackets included, and shows the strings inside in single quotes. `len(tags)` is the number of items, 3, and `len("travel")` is the number of characters, 6.
Because the list was made with double quotes, it is easy to write double quotes in the output too, or to leave out the space after each comma. A string is the same string whichever quotes you make it with, and when you print a list, its strings show up in single quotes.
problems.code:
tags = ["cafe", "travel", "food"]
print(tags)
print(len(tags))
print(len("travel"))
problems.solution:
tags = ["cafe", "travel", "food"]
print(tags)
print(len(tags))
print(len("travel"))

problems.title: An empty list and one empty string
problems.prompt: Here are a drafts folder with nothing written in it yet and a memo list that holds one empty memo. Predict the three lines of output without running the code.
hints: How many items are in `[""]`?
problems.explain:
`drafts` is an empty list with no items, so its length is 0. `memos` holds one item, an empty string, so its length is 1, and when you print it, that empty string shows up as two single quotes.
Since the string inside is empty, it is easy to think the list is empty too and write 0. `len()` only counts the items in a list. It does not care whether an item is empty inside.
problems.code:
drafts = []
memos = [""]
print(len(drafts))
print(len(memos))
print(memos)
problems.solution:
drafts = []
memos = [""]
print(len(drafts))
print(len(memos))
print(memos)

problems.title: A line that reports the post count
problems.prompt: The list `posts` holds post titles. Count the posts and print one line like `Posts: 3`. Calculate the count from the number of items in `posts`. Grading runs the code again with a different `posts` list.
hints: Count the items in a list with `len()`.
You can put `len(posts)` inside the braces of an f-string.
problems.explain:
`len(posts)` counts the items, and the f-string puts that number into the line. If there are no posts at all, it prints `Posts: 0`.
If you write 3 directly, it always prints 3, even when posts are added or removed. If you forget the `f` before the quotes, the braces are printed as plain text, and if you put quotes around the name, as in `len("posts")`, it counts the five letters of the word.
problems.code: posts = ["Cafe review", "Travel photos", "Notice"]
problems.solution:
posts = ["Cafe review", "Travel photos", "Notice"]
print(f"Posts: {len(posts)}")

problems.title: Indexing and slicing a list
problems.prompt: These are the view counts of five posts. Predict the five lines of output without running the code.
hints: The index of the first item is 0. Negative indexes count from the end.
A slice does not include the item at its end index.
problems.explain:
`views[1]` is the second item, 95, and `views[-2]` is the second item from the end, 120. `views[1:3]` is `[95, 480]`, which holds only items 1 and 2, and `views[3:]`, with the end left empty, runs from item 3 to the end. The result of a slice is also a list, so `len()` counts its items: 2.
It is easy to include item 3, which is 120, in `views[1:3]` as well. The number of items in the slice is the end index minus the start index: 3 - 1 = 2. Reading `views[1]` as the first item, 310, is also a common mistake.
problems.code:
views = [310, 95, 480, 120, 260]
print(views[1])
print(views[-2])
print(views[1:3])
print(views[3:])
print(len(views[1:3]))
problems.solution:
views = [310, 95, 480, 120, 260]
print(views[1])
print(views[-2])
print(views[1:3])
print(views[3:])
print(len(views[1:3]))

problems.title: The first two and the last two
problems.prompt: The list of posts is long, so the preview shows only the first two and the last two. Fill in the two blanks. There are always at least four posts, and grading runs the code again with different lists.
hints: A slice with an empty start or end runs from the beginning or to the end. A start position can be negative too.
Both sides of `+` must be lists to join them.
problems.explain:
In the first blank, `posts[:2]` gives items 0 and 1. In the second, `posts[-2:]` gives the items from the second to last to the end. Each is a new list. Joining the two lists with `+` makes the preview, and `posts` stays unchanged.
If you leave out the colon, as in `posts[-2]`, you get a single item instead of a list, and `+` raises a TypeError. If you fix the position, as in `posts[4:]`, the code breaks when the number of posts changes, so count from the end with a negative index.
problems.solution:
posts = ["notice", "cafe", "trip", "food", "gym", "book"]
preview = posts[:2] + posts[-2:]
print(preview)

problems.title: View counts from the second to the fourth post
problems.prompt: This code tries to take the three view counts of the second through fourth posts from the list, store them in `picked`, and print them. It runs without errors, but only two values come out. Fix just one place. Grading runs the code again with different lists.
hints: What is the index of the second post?
The item at the end index of a slice is not included.
problems.explain:
The index of the second post is 1, and the index of the fourth is 3. The item at the end index is not included, so to include index 3, write 4 as the end: `views[1:4]`. Before the fix, `views[2:4]` held only the third and fourth items.
If you keep the start and make the end larger, as in `views[2:5]`, you get three items, but they are the third through the fifth. To turn "the nth item" into an index, subtract 1. For the end index, add 1 to the last index you want to include.
problems.code:
views = [310, 95, 480, 120, 260]
picked = views[2:4]
print(picked)
problems.solution:
views = [310, 95, 480, 120, 260]
picked = views[1:4]
print(picked)

problems.title: Inserting, removing, and popping
problems.prompt: This code changes the list of tags on a post. Predict the two lines of output without running the code.
hints: After `insert(2, "news")`, each item that was at index 2 or later moves up by one index.
If the same value appears more than once, how many of them does `remove()` delete?
problems.explain:
After `insert(2, "news")`, the list is `["cafe", "food", "news", "cafe", "travel"]`. `remove("cafe")` deletes only the first `"cafe"` it finds from the front, and `pop()` takes out the last item, `"travel"`, and returns it. So `last` is travel, and three items remain in `tags`.
It is easy to think that `remove()` deletes every `"cafe"`, or to write that the value `pop()` took out is still in `tags`. `remove()` only finds a value and deletes it, while `pop()` takes out the item at a position and returns its value.
problems.code:
tags = ["cafe", "food", "cafe", "travel"]
tags.insert(2, "news")
tags.remove("cafe")
last = tags.pop()
print(last)
print(tags)
problems.solution:
tags = ["cafe", "food", "cafe", "travel"]
tags.insert(2, "news")
tags.remove("cafe")
last = tags.pop()
print(last)
print(tags)

problems.title: Passing the turn in a question queue
problems.prompt: `queue` is the list of people waiting to ask a question during a live stream. Take the person at the front out of the list and store their name in `now`. Then add the newcomer `"taeo"` to the end of the list. Grading runs the code with a different `queue` list and then checks the values of `now` and `queue`. The list always has at least one person.
hints: If you give `pop()` a position, it takes out the item at that position and returns it. The front position is 0.
The method that adds an item to the end is `append()`.
problems.explain:
`queue.pop(0)` takes the first person out of the list and returns that name, so it goes straight into `now`. Then `append("taeo")` adds the new person to the end of the list.
`pop()` with empty parentheses takes out the last person, and `now = queue[0]` alone reads the name but does not remove it from the list. `remove()` does not return the value it deleted, so `now = queue.remove(queue[0])` cannot get the name.
problems.code: queue = ["mina", "jun", "sora"]
problems.solution:
queue = ["mina", "jun", "sora"]
now = queue.pop(0)
queue.append("taeo")
print(now)
print(queue)

problems.title: An insert with the position and the value swapped
problems.prompt: This code tries to put 45, the number of likes on a post you just uploaded, at the front of the list. It runs without errors, but 45 is not at the front. Fix just one line. Grading runs the code again with different lists.
hints: In what order do you pass the position and the value to `insert()`?
problems.explain:
The order is `insert(position, value)`, so `likes.insert(45, 0)` means "put 0 at position 45." If you give a position past the end of the list, the value is added to the end without an error, so you get `[120, 80, 200, 0]`. If you change it to `likes.insert(0, 45)`, 45 goes into position 0, which is the front.
Passing the two values in the wrong order gives no error, so it is hard to notice until you actually look at the output.
problems.code:
likes = [120, 80, 200]
likes.insert(45, 0)
print(likes)
problems.solution:
likes = [120, 80, 200]
likes.insert(0, 45)
print(likes)

problems.title: What append returns
problems.prompt: Predict the two lines of output without running the code.

problems.title: A new sorted list that leaves the original alone
problems.prompt: Leave `a` as it is, and store in `ranked` a new list that has the numbers of `a` sorted from largest to smallest. The last two lines print `a` and `ranked`.
hints: Which should you use: `sort()`, which changes the list in place, or `sorted()`, which returns a new list?
If you reverse a new list sorted from smallest to largest with `reverse()`, the largest numbers come first.
problems.explain:
`sorted(a)` leaves `a` as it is and returns a new sorted list. Reversing this new list with `reverse()` puts the largest numbers first. `reverse()` reverses the list in place and returns `None`, so if you write it all on one line, as in `ranked = sorted(a).reverse()`, `ranked` gets `None`.
`a.sort()` changes `a` itself and returns `None`, so the first line of output changes. Once you learn keyword arguments in §8.3, you can write this in one line: `sorted(a, reverse=True)`.
problems.code:
a = [40, 70, 90, 60]
# Write your code here
print(a)
print(ranked)
problems.solution:
a = [40, 70, 90, 60]
ranked = sorted(a)
ranked.reverse()
print(a)
print(ranked)

If you put parentheses only around `yesterday / yesterday`, the order of calculation stays the same. In an expression where the subtraction must come first, such as a growth rate, you need parentheses around that subtraction to get the calculation you mean.

hints: `views += 3` is the same as `views = views + 3`.

When `mark` is not given, it uses the default value `"#"`. Keyword arguments go in by name, whatever their order. In `make_tag("@", "ai")` the order is switched, so `word` gets `"@"` and `mark` gets `"ai"`. That is why it prints `ai@` without an error.
The last call, `make_tag()`, has no value for `word`, so it stops with a TypeError. A wrong number of arguments stops the program with an error, but a wrong order does not stop it and gives a wrong value.

def make_tag(word, mark="#"):

print(make_tag("ai", "@"))

problems.title: A false message left by a wide net
problems.prompt: You had a function that computes the follower growth rate (%). You asked an AI, "Fix it so that no errors happen," and got this code. Predict the output without running the code.
hints: What error does `None - 150` raise? Is that error also caught by `except:`?
problems.explain:
The first call is `50 / 200 * 100`, which is 25.0. The second call divides by 0 and raises a ZeroDivisionError; the `except:` with no error name catches it, prints the message, and returns 0. The third call raises a TypeError at `None - 150`, but `except:` catches that too and prints the misleading message that the previous value is 0.
It is easy to predict that the program stops with an error at the third call, but an `except:` with no error name catches every error. So the real cause, the missing data, is hidden, and only a false message and 0 remain. If you narrow it to `except ZeroDivisionError:`, the third call stops with a TypeError and points to the missing data right away.

problems.title: A search for the most likes that stops halfway
problems.prompt: You had a function that finds the largest value in a list of likes stored as text. You asked an AI, "Fix it so that no errors happen," and got this code. It runs without errors, but it prints 120. Fix it so that it reports and skips only the entries that are not numbers, like `Skipped: private`, and prints 300. Write the name of the error to catch after `except`, so that unexpected mistakes, like `None` mixed into the list, still show up as errors.
hints: When `"private"` raises an error, the code leaves the whole loop that `try` wraps.
If you move `try` inside the loop, each entry is tried separately.
problems.explain:
Before the fix, `try` wraps the whole loop, so the moment `"private"` raises a ValueError, the code leaves the loop and finishes having seen only up to 120. The `except:` with no error name and the `pass` covered this up without a word. If you move `try` inside the loop and report the skipped entry under `except ValueError:`, you get 300.
If you move only `try` and leave `except:` as it is, the TypeError from a mixed-in `None` is also handled as `Skipped`, and the problem in the data gets buried. If you ask in turn whether `except` has a name, whether `try` is too wide, and what the code does after catching the error, all three problems come to light.

require.message: Use `try` and an `except` that names the error to skip entries that are not numbers.
